ns1:channel.ns1:title: Nature Human Behaviour
ns1:channel.ns1:description: Drawing from a broad spectrum of social and natural science disciplines, Nature Human Behaviour will publish research of outstanding significance into any aspect of human behaviour, its psychological, biological, and social bases. How do humans perceive, think, feel, decide, and act? How do they interact with their environments and others? How do these abilities develop and decline over the lifespan? How do they evolve and compare with other species? How do they vary among individuals, groups, and cultures? How are they shaped by socioeconomic and political factors? How are they affected by disease or deprivation? What interventions can influence individual behaviours or outcomes? The journal welcomes research from any discipline that provides significant original insight into these questions.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Staying in academia after extended leave
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02594-2

Returning to academia after extended leave often depends on luck and goodwill. We need better and formalized systems to facilitate returns and retention, argues Theresa Mercer.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Loneliness and desire for thinness explain sex differences in adolescent internalizing problems
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02578-2

Girls tend to show higher rates of depression and suicidal ideation than boys. This work suggests that loneliness and pressure to be thin explain much of this gap, suggesting that social factors are key targets for youth-focused support, policy and intervention.
ns1:item.dc:title: Loneliness and desire for thinness explain sex differences in adolescent internalizing problems

ns1:item.ns1:title: Building health-literate artificial intelligence
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02595-1

Can AI do more than deliver health information? This Perspective argues that AI should be designed to support understanding, informed decision-making and action, placing health literacy at the centre of AI design and governance.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02571-9

Before the British invasion in 1788, Australia’s Indigenous population is estimated to have numbered about 2.2 million people, exceeding previous estimates. An estimated 2.06 million excess deaths occurred between 1788 and 1861.
ns1:item.dc:title: Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion

ns1:item.ns1:title: Defining collectivism as duties in relationships rather than generalized warmth improves predictive validity in 100 cultures
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02525-1

Talhelm et al. propose responsibilism as a specific conceptualization of collectivism that emphasizes responsibilities, duties and roles in close relationships. The responsibilism scale effectively captures cross-cultural differences.
ns1:item.dc:title: Defining collectivism as duties in relationships rather than generalized warmth improves predictive validity in 100 cultures
